podcast.title: Skate Punk Founders and Historical Oversight (Around 1978)
podcast.body: The Big Boys, a punk band from Austin, Texas, are credited with largely founding the skate punk sound around 1978. Despite their significant influence on bands like Red Hot Chili Peppers and Sonic Youth, they have often been overlooked in rock history. "Big boy largely founded that sound, skate punk, starting back in around 1978."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lead Singer Randy Biscuit Turner's Open Identity
podcast.body: The band's lead singer, Randy Biscuit Turner, was openly gay and proud of his identity, contributing to the band's trailblazing status within the punk scene. "The lead singer was Randy Biscuit Turner. He was out and he was proud of it."

podcast.title: Red Hot Chili Peppers Admiration
podcast.body: The band Red Hot Chili Peppers were notable fans of Big Boys. "All the members were skaters themselves and the chili peppers ended up being big fans of Big Boys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Skate Rock Compilations
podcast.body: The band appeared on a series of compilation records known as "Skate Rock," which were collections of hard, fast songs intended for skaters to use while practicing their moves on the halfpipe. "They appeared on a series of compilation records called Skate Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Skateboard Culture Presence
podcast.body: Big Boys appeared in skateboard magazines and even had their own custom Big Boys skateboard design, highlighting their close ties to the skateboarding community. "They appeared in skateboard magazines and even had their own custom Big Boys skateboard design."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Skaters and Musical Evolution
podcast.body: Formed in Austin, Texas in 1977, all members of Big Boys were skaters themselves. The band initially played hard, fast punk before evolving towards hardcore with added elements of funk. "All the members were skaters themselves and the chili peppers ended up being big fans of Big Boys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Enduring Popularity (2000s)
xref.body: Pearl Jam is cited as one of the bands from the 1990s that never went away, continuing to be popular with fans and contributing to the difficulty for new artists to break through in the 21st century. "Green Day, Blink-182, Chili Peppers, Pearl Jam, Smashing Pumpkins, Food Fighters, even bands that ceased to exist, Stone Temple Pilots, Nirvana, Beastie Boys, for example, continued to be extremely popular with fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Live Performance Dominance
xref.body: The Foo Fighters were recognized as one of the "big boys" in the alt-rock scene during the latter half of the 2000s. While their music sales were respectable, their primary source of income came from live performances, indicative of a shift in industry economics. "Sales of their music were respectable, but the big paydays came from playing live."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

xref.title: Live Performance Success
xref.body: By 2008, Coldplay was considered one of the "big boys" in the alt-rock universe, along with bands like Foo Fighters, Weezer, Pearl Jam, and U2. They demonstrated their ability to draw massive audiences, selling millions of concert tickets despite comparatively lower record sales in the post-Napster era. "While the big boys, like the Foo Fighters and Coldplay and Weezer and Pearl Jam and you too, continued to do their thing for the latter half of the Zero-Zero's, a couple of trends and movements emerged in the Alt Rock universe."
